The Inevitable Reality (1). What is the Inevitable Reality? (2). And what will make you know what the Inevitable Reality is? (3).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The Inevitable Reality. What is the Inevitable Reality?﴾ It means the Resurrection, and it was named so because matters are realized (taḥuqqu) in it, as al-Tabari said, as if he made it from the pattern of "a sleeping night" (laylun na'im). It was also said: it was named al-Haqqah because it will certainly occur without any doubt. It was also said: it was named so because it made the Garden binding (aḥaqqat) for some peoples, and made the Fire binding for other peoples. It was also said: it was named so because in it every person becomes deserving (ḥaqīq) of the recompense of his deed. Al-Azhari said: It is said "ḥaaqaqtuhu fa-haqaqtuhu uhuquhu," meaning: I contended with him and I prevailed over him. So the Resurrection is al-Haqqah because it establishes against every disputer in the religion of Allah with falsehood, that is, every opponent. In al-Sihah: "wa-haqqahu" means he disputed with him, and each of them claimed the truth; when one prevails over the other it is said "haqqahu." It is said of a man who disputes over trivial matters: "innahu la-naziqu al-ḥiqaq" (he is quick to quarrel). And it is said: "mālahu fīhi ḥaqqun wa-lā ḥiqāq," meaning there is no dispute. Al-tahaqqu means mutual disputing, and al-ihtiqaq means litigation. Al-Haqqah, al-Haqqah and al-Haqq are three dialects with the same meaning. Al-Kisa'i and al-Mawrij said: al-Haqqah is the Day of the Truth. The Arabs say: "lammā ʿarafa al-ḥaqqata minnī harab" (when he recognised the claim against him from me, he fled). The first al-Haqqah is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and the second subject together with its predicate, which is mā al-Haqqah, is the predicate, because its meaning is "what is it." The expression is interrogative, its meaning being glorification and magnification of its matter, just as you say: "Zayd mā Zayd!" as an exaltation of his rank.

(Wa-mā adrāka mā al-Haqqah) is also interrogative, meaning: what has made you know what that Day is? The Prophet (ﷺ) was knowledgeable about the Resurrection, but through its description. So it is said, to magnify its matter: "wa-mā adrāka mā hiya," as if you do not know it, since you have not witnessed it. Yahya ibn Salam said: I have been informed that everything in the Qur'an introduced by "wa-mā adrāka" means He has made him know it and taught him, and everything in which He said "wa-mā yudrīka" is something He did not make him know. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 69, verse 4:

He mentions those who denied the Resurrection. Al-Qari'ah (the Striking Calamity) is the Resurrection, and it was so named because it strikes people (taqra'u al-nas) with its terrors. It is said: "Calamities of time (qawari' al-dahr) befell them," meaning its terrors and its hardships. And we seek refuge in Allah from the qawari' of so-and-so, his lewd remarks (lawadhi'uhu), and the qawarisu of his tongue, the plural of qarisah, which is a harmful word. The qawari' of the Qur'an are the verses which a person recites when he is frightened by jinn or humans, such as the Verse of the Throne (ayat al-Kursi), as though they strike the Shaytan. It is also said: al-qari'ah is derived from the qur'ah (lottery) in raising some people and lowering others; this was said by al-Mubarrad. It is also said: by al-qari'ah is meant the punishment that descended upon them in this world, and their Prophet would warn them of it, but they denied him. Thamud were the people of Salih, and their dwellings were in al-Hijr, between al-Sham and al-Hijaz. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: it is Wadi al-Qura, and they were Arabs ('uruban). As for 'Ad, they were the people of Hud, and their dwellings were in al-Ahqaf. Al-Ahqaf: the sand between 'Oman and Hadramawt and all of Yemen. They were Arabs, possessing physical stature and strength (dhawi khalqin wa basţah), as mentioned by Muhammad ibn Ishaq. This has already been discussed [see vol. 7, p. 236].

Ṭāghiyah (The Overwhelming Blast) — verse 5 of Surah al-Ḥāqqah

There is an ellipsis (iḍmār) in it, meaning: by the overwhelming deed (bi-al-fa'lah al-ṭāghiyah). Qatadah said: meaning, by the overwhelming cry (bi-al-ṣayḥah al-ṭāghiyah), that is, the one exceeding the limit, that is, exceeding the bounds of cries because of the terror. As He said: ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a single cry, and they became like the dried remnant of a fence-builder's enclosure﴾ [al-Qamar: 31]. And ṭughyān (transgression) is exceeding the limit, and from it: ﴿When the water overflowed [beyond its limit]﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah: 11], meaning it exceeded the limit. Al-Kalbi said: "with the ṭāghiyah" means with the thunderbolt (al-ṣā'iqah). Mujahid said: with the sins. Al-Hasan said: with the transgression (al-ṭughyān); so it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) like al-kādhibah, al-'āqibah and al-'āfiyah, meaning they were destroyed because of their transgression and their disbelief. It has also been said that al-ṭāghiyah is the one who hamstrung the she-camel, as Ibn Zayd said, meaning they were destroyed because of what their ṭāghiyah (leader of transgression) committed in hamstringing the she-camel. He was one man, but all of them perished because they approved of his deed and backed it. It has also been said that he was called ṭāghiyah in the same way one says: so-and-so is a rāwiyat al-shi'r (a great transmitter of poetry), a dāhiyah (a shrewd, clever man), an 'allāmah (a great scholar) and a nassābah (a great genealogist).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 69, verse 6–7:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And as for ʿAd, they were destroyed by a violent wind﴾, meaning a cold wind that burns with its coldness like the burning of fire, derived from al-ṣirr, which is cold. This was said by al-Ḍaḥḥak. It was also said: it is the one of intense sound. Mujahid said: it is the one of intense hot winds (al-samum). ﴿Furious﴾, meaning it rebelled against its keepers so that they could not control it, and they could not withstand it because of the severity of its blowing. It became angry at the anger of God. It was also said: it rebelled against ʿAd and overpowered them.

Sufyan al-Thawri narrated from Musa ibn al-Musayyab, from Shahr ibn Hawshab, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God has never sent any soul [[The word in the manuscripts of the original reads "nasafahu" with a fa'. What is in al-Zamakhshari reads "safihu".]] of wind except by a measure, nor any drop of water except by a measure, except on the day of ʿAd and the day of Noah. As for the day of Noah, the water rose over the keepers, and they had no way over it." Then he recited: ﴿Indeed, when the water rose beyond all bounds, We carried you in the sailing ship﴾ [al-Haqqah 69:11]. "And as for the day of ʿAd, the wind rebelled against the keepers, and they had no power over it." Then he recited: ﴿with a violent, furious wind; He imposed it upon them﴾, meaning He sent it and gave it power over them. Taskhir (subjugation) is the employment of a thing with power.

﴿For seven nights and eight days, in succession﴾, meaning continuous, not relenting nor ceasing, from Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Masʿud and others. Al-Farra' said: al-ḥusum means continuous succession, from ḥasm al-dāʾ (cauterizing the disease), when its owner is cauterized with the branding iron and then that is repeated upon him. ʿAbd al-ʿAziz ibn Zurara al-Kilabi said:

"So a time separated between their union, a time in which years followed one another, ḥusum."

Al-Mubarrad said: it is from your saying, ḥasamtu al-shayʾ, when you cut it off and separated it from other things. It was also said: al-ḥasm is uprooting. A sword is called ḥusam because it cuts off the enemy from reaching the goal of his hostility. The poet said:

"A blade which, when you stand supported by it, the one who returns to it needs no beginning, it is not a supporting staff."

The meaning is that it cut them off, that is, severed and removed them. Thus it is the one that cuts with the punishment of uprooting. Ibn Zayd said: it cut them off and left none of them. He also said: it cut off the nights and the days until it covered them entirely.

Because it began at sunrise on the first day and ended at sunset on the last day. Al-Layth said: al-ḥusum means ill omen. It is said: these are the nights of al-ḥusum, that is, they cut off good from their people, as is stated in al-Sihah. ʿIkrima and al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas said: inauspicious, its evidence being His saying, exalted is He: ﴿in inauspicious days﴾ [Fussilat 41:16]. ʿAtiyya al-ʿAwfi: ḥusuman means it cut off good from their people. It has been disputed about their beginning: it was said, the morning of Sunday, said by al-Suddi. It was said, the morning of Friday, said by al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas. It was said, the morning of Wednesday, said by Yahya ibn Sallam and Wahb ibn Munabbih. Wahb said: these are the days which the Arabs call the days of the old woman, with cold and violent wind, and their first was Wednesday and their last was Wednesday. They were attributed to the old woman because an old woman of ʿAd entered a cave, and the wind pursued her and killed her on the eighth day. It was also said: they were called the days of the old woman because they fell in the end of winter, and it is in Adhar, one of the months of the Syriacs. It has well-known names, and concerning it the poet says, and he is Ibn Ahmar: [[In Lisan al-ʿArab, under the root k-s-ʿ, it is attributed to Abu Shibl al-Aʿrabi.]]

"Winter was cut off (kusiʿa) by seven gloomy days, the days of our old woman of the month."

"So when its days ended and passed, Sinn and Sinnabr went along with Wabr."

"And with Amir and his brother Mu'tamir, and Muʿallil, and with the extinguisher of embers."

"Winter departed fleeing hastily, and there came upon you a burning heat from al-Najr [[al-Najr: heat.]]."

Ḥusuman is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥal). It was also said it is an accusative of the verbal noun. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, they cut them off, ḥusuman, that is, they destroy them; it is an emphatic verbal noun. It is also permissible that it be an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), that is, He subjected it upon them for this period for the purpose of uprooting, that is, for cutting them off and uprooting them. It is also permissible that it be the plural of ḥasim. Al-Suddi read ḥusuman with a fatḥa, as a state (ḥal) of the wind, meaning He subjected it upon them uprooting.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then you see the people in it﴾, meaning in those nights and days.

(ṣarʿa) is the plural of ṣarīʿ, meaning dead. It was also said: "in it" means in the wind.

(ka-annahum aʿjāz) means roots.

(nakhlin khāwiya) means decayed, said by Abu al-Tufayl. It was also said: hollow in the trunks, with nothing in them. The word nakhl may be masculine or feminine. He has said elsewhere, exalted is He: ﴿as if they were trunks of palm trees uprooted﴾ [al-Qamar 54:20]. So it is possible that they were likened to palm trees that were felled from their roots, and this is a report of the greatness of their bodies. It is also possible that what is meant is the roots and not the trunks, meaning the wind had cut them off until they became like the roots of palm trees, hollow; that is, the wind used to enter their bodies and fell them like a hollow palm trunk. Ibn Shajara said: the wind used to enter their mouths and expel what was in their bowels of stuffing from their backsides, so they became like hollow palm trees. Yahya ibn Sallam said: He only said hāwiya because their bodies were emptied of their spirits, like hollow palm trees. It is also possible that the meaning is "as if they were the roots of palm trees hollow from their stems in the open ground," as He said: ﴿So those are their houses, empty﴾ [al-Naml 27:52], that is, ruined, with no inhabitants in them. It is also possible that khawiya means decayed, as we have mentioned, because when it decays its interior becomes empty. Thus they were likened, after they perished, to hollow palm trees.

It is also possible that khawiya means decayed, as we have mentioned, because when it decays its interior becomes empty. Thus they were likened, after they perished, to hollow palm trees.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 69, verse 8:

﴿Do you see any remnant of them?﴾ That is, any surviving group (firqah baqiyah) or any surviving soul (nafs baqiyah). It has also been said: "any remnant" (min baqiyyah). And it has been said: "any survival" (min baqa'). Here the form fa'ilah is used in the sense of a verbal noun (masdar), like al-'aqibah (the outcome) and al-'afiyah (well-being). It is also permissible that it be a noun, meaning: "Do you find any one of them remaining?"

Ibn Juraij said: They remained alive for seven nights and eight days in the punishment of Allah by the wind. When they reached evening on the eighth day, they died. Then the wind carried them away and cast them into the sea. This is the meaning of His words, Exalted and Majestic be He: ﴿Do you see any remnant of them?﴾ And His words, Exalted and Majestic be He: ﴿So that not a thing could be seen except their dwellings﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 25] [[See vol. 16, p. 207]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 69, verse 9:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Pharaoh came, and those before him﴾. Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read (wa-man qablahu) with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the ba', meaning "and those with him and following him among his soldiers." Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim chose this reading, taking as evidence the reading of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) and Ubayy (ibn Ka'b): "and those with him" (wa-man ma'ahu). Abu Musa al-Ash'ari read "and those in his presence" (wa-man tilqa'ahu). The rest read qablahu with a fatha on the qaf and a sukun on the ba', meaning "and those who preceded him of the past generations and the bygone nations."

(Wal-mu'tafikat) means the people of the towns of Lot. The common reading is with an alif. Al-Hasan and al-Jahdari read "wal-mu'tafikah" in the singular. Qatadah said: The towns of the people of Lot were only called "mu'tafikat" because they were overturned with their people, that is, they were turned upside down. Al-Tabari reported from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi who said: There were five towns: Sab'ah, Si'rah, A'mrah, Dawma and Sadum, and this was the greatest town.

(Bil-khati'ah) means with the sinful deed, which is disobedience and disbelief. Mujahid said: with the sins they used to commit. Al-Jurjani said: that is, with the great error, so al-khati'ah is a verbal noun (masdar).

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran)

On surah 69, verse 10:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So they disobeyed the messenger of their Lord﴾. Al-Kalbi said: "It is Musa (Moses)." It was also said: "It is Lut (Lot), because he is closer." It was also said: He meant both Musa and Lut, peace be upon them, as He said: ﴿Say: Indeed, we are a messenger of the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 16]. [See vol. 13, p. 93.]

It was also said: "rasul" here means "risalah" (message). The word for the message is sometimes expressed by "rasul," as the poet said: [It is Kuthayyir ʿAzza.]

The slanderers have indeed lied; I did not disclose a secret to them,
nor did I send them as a messenger.

﴿So He seized them with a overwhelming seizing﴾, meaning a high seizing, exceeding other seizings and the punishment of [other] nations. From the same root is "riba" (usury), when one takes more of gold and silver than he gives. It is said: "raba al-shay'u yarbu," meaning it increased and multiplied. Mujahid said: "shadidah" (severe). It seems he meant increased in severity.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an, *The Compendium of the Rulings of the Qur'an*) on surah 69, verses 11–12:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, when the water overflowed﴾, meaning it rose and became high. Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "It overflowed over its keepers from among the angels, in anger for their Lord, so they were unable to hold it back." Qatadah said: "It rose fifteen cubits above everything." Ibn Abbas said: "In the time of Nuh the water overflowed its keepers, and it increased over them, so they did not know how much came out." No drop of water descends before it or after it except by a known measure, other than on that day. This has already been related with a traced-back (marfu') chain at the beginning of the surah.

The purpose of narrating the stories of these nations and mentioning the punishment that befell them is to warn this Ummah against imitating them in disobeying the Messenger. Then He bestowed a favour upon them by making them the offspring of those who were saved from drowning, by His saying: ﴿We carried you﴾, meaning We carried your fathers while you were in their loins.

(﴿In the sailing ship﴾), meaning in the sailing ships. Those carried in the ship were Nuh and his sons, and everyone on the face of the earth from the descendants of those.

(﴿So that We might make it a reminder for you﴾)

That is, the ship of Nuh, upon him be blessings and peace. Allah made it a reminder and a lesson for this Ummah, so that its earliest generations came to see it, according to the view of Qatadah. Ibn Jurayj said: "Its planks were on al-Judi." The meaning is: We preserved for you those timbers so that you would remember what befell the people of Nuh and Allah's saving of your fathers, and how many ships have perished and turned to dust, leaving nothing of them. It was also said: "So that We might make that deed, the drowning of the people of Nuh and the saving of those who believed with him, an admonition for you." For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And an attentive ear will heed it﴾, meaning an ear that retains and listens to what has come from Allah, preserving it. The ship cannot be described by this. Al-Zajjaj said: "It is said: 'I retained such-and-such' (wa'aytu kadha), meaning I preserved it within myself; I retain it, wa'yan. Wa'aytu al-ilm (I retained the knowledge), wa'aytu ma qulta (I retained what you said), all have the same meaning. Awaytu al-mata' fi al-wi'a' (I put the goods into the container)." Al-Zajjaj said: "For whatever you have preserved outside yourself, one says awaytuhu (with an alif), and for what you have preserved within yourself, one says wa'aytuhu (without an alif)."

Talhah, Humayd and al-A'raj recited ﴿wa-ta'iyaha﴾ with a sukun on the letter ayn (ta'iyaha, with the 'ayn silent), by analogy with the saying ﴿arina﴾ (show us) in His words: ﴿And show us our rites﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:128]. Scholars differed on this reading as transmitted from Asim and Ibn Kathir. The rest read it with a kasrah on the ayn, which parallels His saying: ﴿and an attentive ear will heed it﴾. [See the commentary on this verse in volume 17, page 23] Regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart﴾ [Qaf 50:37].

Qatadah said: "The attentive ear is an ear that understood from Allah the Exalted and benefited from what it heard of the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic."

Makhul related that when this verse was revealed, the Prophet ﷺ said: "I asked my Lord to make it the ear of Ali." Makhul said: "Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, used to say: 'I never heard anything from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and then forgot it, but I retained it.'" Al-Mawardi mentioned this. Similarly from al-Hasan, mentioned by al-Tha'labi, who said: When ﴿and an attentive ear will heed it﴾ was revealed, the Prophet ﷺ said: "I asked my Lord to make it your ear, O Ali." Ali said: "By Allah, I have forgotten nothing since, and it was not for me to forget." Abu Barzah al-Aslami said: The Prophet ﷺ said to Ali: "O Ali, indeed Allah commanded me to bring you near and not push you away, and to teach you, and that you should retain, and it is the right of Allah that you retain."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 69, verse 15–17:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So on that Day the Inevitable Event will occur﴾, meaning the Resurrection will come to pass.

(And the sky will be split asunder), meaning it will be cleft and torn apart. It is also said: it will split because of the descent of the angels within it. The evidence is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the day the sky will be split open with clouds, and the angels will be sent down, descending﴾ [al-Furqan: 25], and this has already been discussed [see vol. 13, p. 23].

(And it, that Day, will be frail), meaning weak. It is said: "al-binaʾ wahā, yahī, wahyan, fahuwa wāh" (the building became weak) when it becomes very feeble. And it is said: "kalam wāh" (a feeble speech), meaning weak. It has been said: after its firmness, it will become like wool in its flimsiness, and this will be because of the descent of the angels, as we mentioned. It has also been said: it is because of the terror of the Day of Resurrection. And it has been said: wāhiyah means torn apart, as Ibn Shajarah said, derived from their saying: "wahiya al-siqaʾ" (the waterskin tore) when it ruptured. And among their proverbs:

Leave the way of one whose waterskin has torn,
And whose water has been spilled in the desert,

meaning: one who is weak of intellect and cannot protect himself.

(And the angels) meaning the angels, a collective noun.

(Upon its borders), meaning upon its edges when it splits, because the sky is their place, according to Ibn ʿAbbas. Al-Mawardi said: this is perhaps also the view of Mujahid and Qatadah. Al-Tha'labi related it from al-Dahhak, who said: upon its edges, of that part which has not split.

The meaning is that the sky is the place of the angels, so when it splits they will be at its edges. Said Saʿid ibn Jubayr: the meaning is that the angels will be upon the rims of the world, that is, they will descend to the earth and guard its edges. It has also been said: when the sky becomes pieces, the angels will stand upon those pieces that have not split in themselves. And it has been said: when people see Hell it will terrify them, so they will flee as camels flee, and they will not come to any region of the earth without finding angels, so they will return from whence they came. And it has been said: upon its borders, awaiting what they are commanded regarding the people of the Fire, of driving them toward it, and regarding the people of Paradise, of greeting and honor. All of this returns to the meaning of Ibn Jubayr's statement. It is supported by His saying: ﴿And the angels will be sent down, descending﴾ [al-Furqan: 25], and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O assembly of jinn and mankind, if you are able to pass beyond the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass; you will not pass except with authority﴾ [al-Rahman: 33], as we have explained there. And al-arjaʾ means the sides and regions in the dialect of Hudhayl; its singular is raja, with a short vowel at the end, and its dual is rajawan, like ʿasa and ʿasawan. The poet said:

So let it not be said of me that the two sides (of the well) ... are the least of the people whose place can be filled by me.

And the word is used for the rim of a well and of a grave.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And upon that Day eight will bear the Throne of your Lord above them﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: eight rows of angels, whose number none knows but Allah. Ibn Zayd said: they are eight angels. From al-Hasan: Allah knows how many they are, eight or eight thousand. It is related from the Prophet ﷺ: "The bearers of the Throne today are four; when the Day of Resurrection comes, Allah, exalted is He, will strengthen them with four others, and they will be eight." Al-Tha'labi mentioned it. Al-Mawardi related it from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Today four bear it, and on the Day of Resurrection they will be eight." Al-ʿAbbas ibn ʿAbd al-Malik said: they are eight angels in the form of wild goats (awʿal) [the awʿal: the mountain male goat]. He related this from the Prophet ﷺ. And in a hadith: "Each of them has four faces: the face of a man, the face of a lion, the face of an ox, and the face of an eagle, and each face asks Allah for provision for that kind." When the verse of Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt was recited before the Prophet ﷺ:

A man and an ox beneath the right foot of Him,
the eagle for the other, and a lion lying in wait,

and:

The sun rises every last night
red, its color blooming, dawning,
it does not appear to them in its course
except punished, or else whipped.

The Prophet ﷺ said: "He has spoken truly." And in a report: "Above the seventh heaven are eight wild goats, between whose hooves and knees is the distance between one heaven and another, and above their backs is the Throne." Al-Qushayri mentioned it, and al-Tirmidhi transmitted it from the hadith of al-ʿAbbas ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib. It has already been given in full in Surah al-Baqarah [see vol. 1, p. 259]. Al-Tha'labi mentioned something similar, and its wording is his. And in a marfuʿ hadith: "The bearers of the Throne are eight angels in the form of wild goats, the distance between their hooves and their knees being a seventy-year journey for a swift bird." In the Tafsir of al-Kalbi: eight parts out of nine parts of the angels. And from him: eight parts out of ten parts of the angels. Then he mentioned the number of the angels at length, which is too long to recount. Al-Tha'labi related the first from him, and al-Qushayri the second. Al-Mawardi said, from Ibn ʿAbbas: eight parts out of nine, and they are the Karubiyyun (the Cherubim) [the Karubiyyun: the masters of the angels, the honored ones, from karb, meaning nearness]. The meaning is that it descends upon the Throne. Then the attribution of the Throne to Allah, exalted is He, is like the attribution of the House (Kaʿbah), and the House is not for dwelling, so likewise the Throne. And the meaning of ﴿above them﴾ is above their heads. Al-Suddi said: the Throne is borne by the bearing angels above them, and none bears the bearers of the Throne except Allah. It has also been said: ﴿above them﴾ means the bearers of the Throne are above the angels who are in the sky upon its borders. It has also been said: ﴿above them﴾ means above the people of the Resurrection.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 69, verse 15–17:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So on that Day the Inevitable Event will occur﴾, meaning the Resurrection will come to pass.

(And the sky will be split asunder), meaning it will be cleft and torn apart. It is also said: it will split because of the descent of the angels within it. The evidence is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the day the sky will be split open with clouds, and the angels will be sent down, descending﴾ [al-Furqan: 25], and this has already been discussed [see vol. 13, p. 23].

(And it, that Day, will be frail), meaning weak. It is said: "al-binaʾ wahā, yahī, wahyan, fahuwa wāh" (the building became weak) when it becomes very feeble. And it is said: "kalam wāh" (a feeble speech), meaning weak. It has been said: after its firmness, it will become like wool in its flimsiness, and this will be because of the descent of the angels, as we mentioned. It has also been said: it is because of the terror of the Day of Resurrection. And it has been said: wāhiyah means torn apart, as Ibn Shajarah said, derived from their saying: "wahiya al-siqaʾ" (the waterskin tore) when it ruptured. And among their proverbs:

Leave the way of one whose waterskin has torn,
And whose water has been spilled in the desert,

meaning: one who is weak of intellect and cannot protect himself.

(And the angels) meaning the angels, a collective noun.

(Upon its borders), meaning upon its edges when it splits, because the sky is their place, according to Ibn ʿAbbas. Al-Mawardi said: this is perhaps also the view of Mujahid and Qatadah. Al-Tha'labi related it from al-Dahhak, who said: upon its edges, of that part which has not split.

The meaning is that the sky is the place of the angels, so when it splits they will be at its edges. Said Saʿid ibn Jubayr: the meaning is that the angels will be upon the rims of the world, that is, they will descend to the earth and guard its edges. It has also been said: when the sky becomes pieces, the angels will stand upon those pieces that have not split in themselves. And it has been said: when people see Hell it will terrify them, so they will flee as camels flee, and they will not come to any region of the earth without finding angels, so they will return from whence they came. And the word is used for the rim of a well and of a grave.

A man and an ox beneath the right foot of Him,
the eagle for the other, and a lion lying in wait,

and:

The sun rises every last night
red, its color blooming, dawning,
it does not appear to them in its course
except punished, or else whipped.

The Prophet ﷺ said: "He has spoken truly." Then he mentioned the number of the angels at length, which is too long to recount. Al-Tha'labi related the first from him, and al-Qushayri the second. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 69, verse 18:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿On that Day you will be presented [for judgment]﴾, meaning before Allah. Its evidence is His saying: "They will be presented before your Lord in rows" [Surah al-Kahf 18:48].

That is not a presentation by which He comes to know what He did not already know; rather, its meaning is reckoning and the affirming of deeds upon them for the sake of recompense. Al-Hasan narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "People will be presented on the Day of Resurrection three times. As for two of the presentations, they will be disputation and excuses. **Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 69, verses 19–34:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿As for him who is given his record in his right hand﴾. Being given the record in the right hand is a sign of salvation. Ibn 'Abbas said: The first person of this Ummah to be given his record in his right hand will be 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, and he will have a radiance like the radiance of the sun. It was said to him: "Where then is Abu Bakr?" He said: "Far, far away! The angels will escort him to Paradise." This was related by al-Tha'labi. We have already mentioned it as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet ﷺ) report from the hadith of Zayd ibn Thabit, in its wording and meaning, in the book "al-Tadhkirah." And praise be to Allah.

﴿He will say: "Here, read my record!"﴾ That is, he will say this out of confidence in his safety and joy at his deliverance, because in the Arabs' usage the right hand is a sign of joy and the left a sign of grief. The poet said: [it is by Ibn al-Dumaynah]

"Tell me, have you placed me in your right hand, so that I rejoice, or have you put me in your left?"

The meaning of "hā'um" is "come here," as said by Ibn Zayd. Muqatil said it means "hallum" (come, bring). It was also said it means "take," and from this is the report on usury: "(only hā' and hā')," meaning each one says to his companion: "Take." Ibn al-Sikkit and al-Kisa'i said: The Arabs say "hā' yā rajul, iqra'" (to a man), for two "hā'umā yā rajulān," for men "hā'umū yā rijāl," and for a woman "hā'ī" (with a kasra on the hamzah), "hā'umā," and "hā'una." The original form is "hā kum," and the hamzah was substituted for the kaf, as said by al-Qutaybi. [There are other dialectal forms, so refer to the lexicon books.] It was also said that "hā'um" is a word established for responding to one who calls, when one is energetic and joyful. It is related that a Bedouin called out to the Prophet ﷺ in a loud voice, and the Prophet ﷺ answered him: "Hā'um," prolonging his voice.

"Kitābiyah" is governed by "hā'um" according to the Kufans, and according to the Basrans by "iqra'ū," since it is the nearer of the two governing words. The original is "kitābī," and the hā' was added to show the fatha of the yā'. The hā' is for pausing (waqf). The same applies to its counterparts: "ḥisābiyah," "māliyah," "sulṭāniyah," and in al-Qari'ah, "mā hiyah." The common recitation (qira'at al-'āmmah) has the hā' in these words both in pause and in continuous reading (wasl), because they are written with the hā' in the muṣḥaf, so it is not to be dropped. Abu 'Ubayd preferred deliberately to pause on them, so as to conform to the language in adding the hā' in pausal sakt (a brief pause) and to conform to the script. Ibn Muhaysin, Mujahid, Humayd and Ya'qub recited with the hā' omitted in continuous reading and affirmed in pause, in these words collectively. Hamzah agreed with them in "māliyah," "sulṭāniyah," and "mā hiyah" in al-Qari'ah. The total of these letters is seven. Abu Hatim preferred the recitation of Ya'qub and those with him, following the language. As for one who recites them in continuous reading with the hā', it is on the intention of pausing.

﴿Indeed I had thought﴾, that is, I was certain and knew, according to Ibn 'Abbas and others. It was also said: that is, "I had thought that if Allah should call me to account for my evil deeds He would punish me," but He has graciously pardoned me with His forgiveness and has not held me to account for them. Al-Dahhak said: Every "ẓann" (thought/supposition) in the Qur'an from a believer is certainty, and from an unbeliever it is doubt. Mujahid said: The thought of the Hereafter is certainty, and the thought of this world is doubt. Al-Hasan said concerning this verse: The believer thought well of his Lord, so he did good deeds, and the hypocrite thought ill of his Lord, so he did evil deeds.

﴿That I would meet my reckoning﴾, that is, in the Hereafter, and he did not deny resurrection. The meaning is that he was saved only through his fear of the Day of Reckoning, because he was certain that Allah would call him to account, so he worked for the Hereafter.

﴿So he will be in a pleasing life﴾, that is, in a life which he finds pleasing, with nothing disagreeable in it. Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Farra' said: "Rāḍiyah" means "marḍiyyah" (pleased with), like your saying "māʾ dāfiq," meaning "madfūq" (poured). It was also said: "dhāt riḍan," meaning its owner is pleased with it, like "laban" and "tamr" (meaning the owner of milk and dates). In the Sahih it is related from the Prophet ﷺ: "They will live and never die; they will be healthy and never fall ill; they will enjoy comfort and never see misery; and they will be young and never grow old." ﴿In a lofty Garden﴾, that is, great in the souls.

﴿Its clusters are near at hand﴾, that is, near for picking; the standing one, the sitting one and the reclining one can all reach them, as will be explained in Surah "al-Insan" [see vol. 19, p. 134]. "Quṭūf" is the plural of "qiṭf" (with a kasra on the qaf), which is what is picked of fruit. "Qaṭf" (with a fatha) is the verbal noun, and "qiṭāf" (with fatha or kasra) is the time of picking.

﴿"Eat and drink"﴾, that is, it will be said to them.

﴿Wholesome﴾, with no troubling and no disturbance in it.

﴿For what you sent forth﴾, that is, what you advanced of righteous deeds.

﴿In the days that are past﴾, that is, in the world. He said "kulū" (eat) after His saying "fa-huwa fī 'īshatin rāḍiyah" because of His saying "fa-ammā man ūtiya," and "man" implies the meaning of plurality.

Al-Dahhak mentioned that this verse was revealed concerning Abu Salamah 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Asad al-Makhzumi, and Muqatil said the same. The verse that follows it concerns his brother al-Aswad ibn 'Abd al-Asad, according to Ibn 'Abbas and also al-Dahhak, as related by al-Tha'labi. This man and his brother are the cause of the revelation of these verses. The meaning is general, encompassing all the people of misery and all the people of happiness, as indicated by His saying: "Eat and drink." It has also been said that what is meant by this is everyone who was followed in good or in evil. If a man was a leader in good, calling to it and commanding it, and many followed him in it, he is called by his name and his father's name, and he advances until, when he draws near, a white record with white writing is brought out for him, in whose inside are the evil deeds and on whose outside are the good deeds. He begins with the evil deeds and reads them, becomes fearful, his face turns pale and his color changes. When he reaches the end of the record he finds in it: "These are your evil deeds, and I have forgiven you." He rejoices greatly at that. Then he turns over his record and reads his good deeds, and he only increases in joy. When he reaches the end of the record he finds in it: "These are your good deeds, which have been multiplied for you." His face becomes bright, a crown is brought and placed upon his head, he is clothed in two garments, and every joint of him is adorned. He grows to sixty cubits, which is the stature of Adam ﷺ (peace be upon him). It is said to him: "Go to your companions, inform them and give them good news that each one of them has the like of this." When he turns away, he says: "Here, read my record! Indeed I had thought that I would meet my reckoning." Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So he will be in a pleasing life﴾, that is, a life that is pleasing, which He has found pleasing, ﴿in a lofty Garden﴾ in the heaven, ﴿its clusters are near at hand﴾: its fruits and its bunches. ﴿Near at hand﴾: brought near to them. He says to his companions: "Do you recognize me?" They say: "Surely you have been overwhelmed by honor. Who are you?" He says: "I am so-and-so, son of so-and-so, and I give each one of you good news of the like of this." ﴿"Eat and drink, wholesome, for what you sent forth in the days that are past"﴾, that is, what you advanced in the days of the world.

And if the man was a leader in evil, calling to it and commanding it, and many followed him in it, he is called by his name and his father's name, and he advances to his reckoning. A black record in black writing is brought out for him, in whose inside are the good deeds and on whose outside are the evil deeds. He begins with the good deeds and reads them, thinking that he will be saved. When he reaches the end of the record he finds in it: "These are your good deeds, and they have been returned to you." His face turns black, grief overcomes him, and he despairs of good. Then he turns over his record and reads his evil deeds, and he only increases in grief, and his face only grows blacker. When he reaches the end of the record he finds in it: "These are your evil deeds, and they have been multiplied against you"; that is, the punishment is multiplied for him. The meaning is not that anything is added to him which he did not do. [He said:] He is then made huge for the Fire, his eyes turn blue, his face blackens, he is clothed in garments of pitch, and it is said to him: "Go to your companions and inform them that each one of them has the like of this." He goes off saying: ﴿"Would that I had not been given my record, and had not known what my reckoning is! Would that it had been the end!"﴾ He wishes for death.

﴿"My authority has perished from me"﴾. The tafsir (explanation) of Ibn 'Abbas: "My proof has perished from me." This is also the view of Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, al-Suddi and al-Dahhak. Ibn Zayd said: It means his authority in the world, which is kingship. This man was obeyed among his companions. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿"Seize him and shackle him"﴾. It was said: A hundred thousand angels will rush to him, then his hand will be joined to his neck, and this is His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿"Shackle him"﴾, that is, bind him with fetters. ﴿"Then roast him in the Blazing Fire"﴾, that is, make him burn in the Blazing Fire. ﴿"Then bind him in a chain whose length is seventy cubits"﴾. Allah knows by which cubit, as said by al-Hasan. Ibn 'Abbas said: Seventy cubits by the cubit of the angel. Nawf said: Each cubit is seventy spans, and each span is further than the distance between you and Makkah. It was in the courtyard of Kufa. Muqatil said: If one link of it were placed on the peak of a mountain, it would melt just as lead melts. Ka'b said: One link of the chain which Allah the Exalted described as seventy cubits in length is equal to all the iron of the world.

﴿Then thread him﴾. Sufyan said: We have been told that it enters through his anus until it comes out of his mouth. Muqatil said the same. The meaning is: "Then thread a chain into him." It was also said: His neck is put through it and then it is pulled tight. It has come in a report that it enters from his anus and comes out through his nostrils. In another report: it enters through his mouth and comes out of his anus. Then he calls to his companions: "Do you recognize me?" They say: "No, but we see what disgrace you are in. Who are you?" He calls to his companions: "I am so-and-so, son of so-and-so; each one of you has the like of this." I say: This interpretation is the most correct of what has been said concerning this verse, as indicated by His saying: ﴿"The Day We shall call every people with their leader"﴾ [see vol. 10, p. 396] [al-Isra': 71]. On this subject there is a hadith from Abu Hurayrah with the same meaning, which al-Tirmidhi recorded. We have mentioned it in Surah "Subhan" [see vol. 10, p. 396], so reflect upon it there.

﴿"Indeed he did not believe in Allah, the Mighty, and did not urge the feeding of the needy"﴾, that is, urging the giving of food, just as "al-'aṭā'" (the giving) is used in place of "al-i'ṭā'" (the giving). The poet said:

"Disbelief after death was turned back from me, and after your giving, the grazing she-camels..." [The verse is from a qasidah of al-Qutami praising Zufar ibn al-Harith al-Kilabi. Ibn Qutaybah said in al-Shi'r wa al-Shu'ara': "Zufar had captured al-Qutami in the war between Qays and Taghlib, and Qays wanted to kill him, but Zufar stood between them and granted him freedom, gave him a hundred camels and released him, so he said: 'Disbelief after...' etc." "Al-ratā'" (with a kasra on the ra') means the grazing ones. See Khizanat al-Adab, the 599th witness.] He meant "after your giving." Thus it is made clear that he was punished for not feeding and for commanding stinginess, just as he was punished for disbelief. "Al-ḥaḍḍ" means urging and inciting. The original construction of "ṭa'ām" is that it should be in the accusative governed by the implied verbal noun. "Ṭa'ām" is an expression for the thing itself, and it is annexed to "miskīn" (the needy) because of the connection between them. Whoever makes "ṭa'ām" operate as "i†ʿām" (feeding) operates, then the position of "miskīn" is accusative. The estimated meaning is "upon feeding the feeder the needy," so the agent is deleted and the verbal noun is annexed to its object.

Ibn Zayd said: It means his authority in the world, which is kingship. This man was obeyed among his companions. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿"Seize him and shackle him"﴾. It was said: A hundred thousand angels will rush to him, then his hand will be joined to his neck, and this is His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿"Shackle him"﴾, that is, bind him with fetters. ﴿"Then roast him in the Blazing Fire"﴾, that is, make him burn in the Blazing Fire. ﴿"Then bind him in a chain whose length is seventy cubits"﴾. Allah knows by which cubit, as said by al-Hasan. Ibn 'Abbas said: Seventy cubits by the cubit of the angel. Nawf said: Each cubit is seventy spans, and each span is further than the distance between you and Makkah. It was in the courtyard of Kufa. Muqatil said: If one link of it were placed on the peak of a mountain, it would melt just as lead melts. Ka'b said: One link of the chain which Allah the Exalted described as seventy cubits in length is equal to all the iron of the world.

﴿Then thread him﴾. Sufyan said: We have been told that it enters through his anus until it comes out of his mouth. Muqatil said the same. The meaning is: "Then thread a chain into him." It was also said: His neck is put through it and then it is pulled tight. It has come in a report that it enters from his anus and comes out through his nostrils. In another report: it enters through his mouth and comes out of his anus. Then he calls to his companions: "Do you recognize me?" They say: "No, but we see what disgrace you are in. Who are you?" ﴿"Indeed he did not believe in Allah, the Mighty, and did not urge the feeding of the needy"﴾, that is, urging the giving of food, just as "al-'aṭā'" (the giving) is used in place of "al-i'ṭā'" (the giving). The poet said:

Ibn Qutaybah said in al-Shi'r wa al-Shu'ara': "Zufar had captured al-Qutami in the war between Qays and Taghlib, and Qays wanted to kill him, but Zufar stood between them and granted him freedom, gave him a hundred camels and released him, so he said: 'Disbelief after...' etc." "Al-ratā'" (with a kasra on the ra') means the grazing ones. Thus it is made clear that he was punished for not feeding and for commanding stinginess, just as he was punished for disbelief. "Al-ḥaḍḍ" means urging and inciting. The original construction of "ṭa'ām" is that it should be in the accusative governed by the implied verbal noun. "Ṭa'ām" is an expression for the thing itself, and it is annexed to "miskīn" (the needy) because of the connection between them. Whoever makes "ṭa'ām" operate as "i†ʿām" (feeding) operates, then the position of "miskīn" is accusative. The estimated meaning is "upon feeding the feeder the needy," so the agent is deleted and the verbal noun is annexed to its object.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So he has no close friend here today﴾. The predicate of "falaysa" is "lahu" (for him); "hahuna" cannot be the predicate, because the meaning would become "there is no food here except from ghislin," and that is not correct, since there is other food. "Hahuna" is attached to the sense of verbal action contained in "lahu." "Al-hamim" here means the near relative, i.e., he has no relative who feels tender toward him and defends him. It is derived from "al-hamim," which is hot water, as if he were a friend whose heart is softened and burns for him. "Al-ghislin" is on the pattern "fi'lin" from "al-ghasl" (washing), as if it washes off from their bodies; it is the pus of the people of the Fire flowing from their wounds and private parts, according to Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Dahhak and al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: it is a tree that the people of the Fire eat. Al-ghisl (with a kasra) is what the head is washed with, such as khatmi and other things. Al-Akhfash said: from it comes "al-ghislin," which is what has been washed off the flesh and blood of the people of the Fire. The ya' and nun were added to it as they were added in "'Ifrin." Qatadah said: it is the worst and most repulsive food. Ibn Zayd said: it is not known what it is, nor is al-zaqqum. He said in another place: ﴿They have no food except from *dari'*﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 6], and it is possible that *dari'* is from al-ghislin. It was also said: there is inversion in the speech, and the meaning is: "So he has no close friend here today, except from ghislin," and it would be hot water. And "nor any food," i.e., they have no food from which they benefit.

﴿None eats it except the sinners﴾, i.e., the guilty. Ibn 'Abbas said: it means the polytheists. It is read *al-khati'un* with the hamza changed to a ya', and *al-khatu'un* with it dropped. It is also possible that it means those who step from truth to falsehood and transgress the limits of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 69, verses 38–40:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So I swear by what you see, and by what you do not see.﴾ The meaning is: I swear by all things, what you see of them and what you do not see. The "lā" (in fa-lā uqsimu) is extra (ṣilah, a particle with no independent semantic force). It has also been said that it is a rejection (radd) of a statement that preceded, meaning: the matter is not as the polytheists say. Muqatil said: the reason for this is that al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah said, "Muhammad is a sorcerer." Abu Jahl said, "He is a poet." And Uqbah said, "He is a soothsayer." So Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿So I swear﴾, meaning, I swear. It has also been said that "fa-lā" here is a negation of the oath, meaning: there is no need for an oath in this matter because the truth in it is clear. On this view, its response (jawab) is like the response of an oath.

﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble Messenger﴾, meaning the Qur'an. It is said that the Messenger here is Jibril (Gabriel), as said by al-Hasan, al-Kalbi and Muqatil. Their evidence is: ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble Messenger, possessed of power, with standing before the Lord of the Throne﴾ [At-Takwir: 19–20]. Al-Kalbi and also al-Qutabi said: the Messenger here is Muhammad (ﷺ), based on His saying: ﴿And it is not the word of a poet﴾. The Qur'an is not the word of the Messenger (ﷺ); it is rather the word of Allah, mighty and majestic. The word was attributed to the Messenger because he recites it, conveys it, and acts upon it, as when we say: "This is the opinion of Malik."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 69, verse 41–42:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Nor is it the word of a poet﴾, because it is entirely distinct from all the kinds of poetry.

(Nor the word of a soothsayer) because it came in dispute with the devils and their reviling, so they do not bring down anything upon one who reviles them. The particle "ma" is extra (za'idah) in His saying: ﴿Little is it that you believe﴾ and ﴿Little is it that you remember﴾, and the meaning is: "Little do you believe, and little do you remember." That little of their belief is that when they are asked who created them, they say: "Allah." It is not permissible that "ma" with the verb be a verbal noun (masdar) such that "qalilan" is governed by what follows "ma", because this would involve placing the relative clause (silah) before the relative pronoun (mawsul), since what the verbal noun governs is part of the clause of the verbal noun.

Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub read (ma yu'minun) and (yadhdhakkarun) with the letter ya'. The rest read them with ta', because the address comes both before and after it. As for what comes before it, it is His saying: ﴿you see﴾ (tubsirun); and as for what comes after it, it is: ﴿so not one of you﴾ (fa-ma minkum), and the verse that follows.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 69, verse 44–46:

Allah's statement: ﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings﴾. Taqawwala (فَقَوَّلَ) means he exerted himself and came up with a saying from his own self. It is also recited as (وَلَوْ تُقُوِّلَ) in the passive voice.

(﴿We would have seized him by the right hand﴾) means: with strength and power, i.e., We would have seized him with force. Min (مِنْ) here is an extra (ziyadah) particle. The right hand is used to express strength and power because the strength of everything lies in its right side, as stated by al-Qutabi, and this is the meaning of the saying of Ibn Abbas and Mujahid. From this is the verse of al-Shammakh:

When a banner is raised for glory... ʿArabah receives it with the right hand

That is, with strength. ʿArabah is the name of a man [[He is ʿArabah ibn Aws ibn Qaydhi al-Awsi al-Harithi al-Ansari, one of the famous generous lords of Madinah. He lived during the time of the Prophet ﷺ, embraced Islam as a child, and died in Madinah around the year sixty (AH).]] from the Ansar, from the Aws. Another poet said: "When I saw the sun, its light shining, I took my need from it with my right hand."

Al-Suddi and al-Hakam said: "with the right hand" means "with the truth." He cited: "ʿArabah receives it with the right hand," meaning "with entitlement."

Al-Hasan said: "We would have cut off his right hand." It was also said: the meaning is "We would have restrained him with His right hand from acting," as stated by Nafṭawayh. Abu Jaʿfar al-Tabari said: this statement came in the manner of humiliation, following the custom of people in seizing the hand of one who is to be punished, as a ruler says to one he wishes to humiliate: "Seize his hands," meaning, "We would have ordered that his hand be seized and We would have intensified his punishment."

(﴿Then We would have severed from him the aorta﴾) meaning the al-watin (الْوَتِين), the sinews of the heart, i.e., We would have destroyed him. It is a vessel on which the heart depends; when it is severed, its owner dies. This was stated by Ibn Abbas and most people. It was said: "When you deliver me and carry my saddle, ʿArabah, then choke on the blood of the watin."

Mujahid said: it is the cord of the heart which is in the back, and it is the spinal cord; when it is severed, the powers are nullified and its owner dies. Al-mu'tawan is the one whose watin has been cut. Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: it is the heart and its membranes and what surrounds it. Al-Kalbi said: it is a vein between the al-ʿilbaʾ and the throat. Al-ʿilbaʾ is the sinew of the neck; there are two ʿilbaʾs, between which the vein grows. Ikrimah said: when the watin is severed, one does not recognize whether one is hungry or full.

(﴿Then We would have severed from him the aorta﴾) meaning the al-watin (الْوَتِين), the sinews of the heart, i.e., We would have destroyed him. It is a vessel on which the heart depends; when it is severed, its owner dies. This was stated by Ibn Abbas and most people. It was said: "When you deliver me and carry my saddle, ʿArabah, then choke on the blood of the watin."

Mujahid said: it is the cord of the heart which is in the back, and it is the spinal cord; when it is severed, the powers are nullified and its owner dies. Al-mu'tawan is the one whose watin has been cut. Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: it is the heart and its membranes and what surrounds it. Al-Kalbi said: it is a vein between the al-ʿilbaʾ and the throat. Al-ʿilbaʾ is the sinew of the neck; there are two ʿilbaʾs, between which the vein grows. Ikrimah said: when the watin is severed, one does not recognize whether one is hungry or full.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 69, verse 47–48:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So none of you could withhold Him from it.﴾ Fa-ma (so not) is a negation, and aḥad (anyone) here carries the sense of the plural, which is why he described it with the plural (ḥājizīn, "withholding"). That is, "there is none of you, a group, who could withhold Him from it." This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 285]. This is plural, because bayna (between) is used only with two or more. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Spoils of war were not made lawful for anyone with black heads before you." Its wording is singular but its meaning is plural. Min (of) is extra (ziyadah).

Al-hajz (withholding) means al-man' (prevention). Ḥājizīn may be an attribute of aḥad according to the meaning mentioned above, in which case it is in the genitive position. The predicate is minkum (of you). It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative, as a predicate, with minkum being superfluous (mulgha) and attached to ḥājizīn. Placing it between does not prevent the predicate from being in the accusative in this case, just as placing it does not prevent it in "inna fika Zaydan raghib" (indeed, in you is Zayd, eager).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed it﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿is a reminder for the God-fearing﴾, that is, for those who fear, who are conscious of Allah. Its parallel is: ﴿In it is guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2], as we explained at the beginning of surat al-Baqarah. It has been said: the intended meaning is Muhammad ﷺ, that is, he is a reminder, a mercy, and a deliverance.

It has also been said: he attached it to itself because the two words differ (in form).
